From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The **[Ivor Novello Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards "Ivor Novello Awards")** are held annually since 1956 by the [Ivors Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ivors_Academy "The Ivors Academy"), formerly the British Academy of Songwriters, Composers and Authors, to recognize the excellence in [songwriting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songwriting "Songwriting") and [composing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_composition "Musical composition"). The following list consists of all the winners and nominees of the awards by year, the winners are listed first and in **bold** followed by the nominees if present.

The awards and nominations are received by the songwriters of the nominated work, not the performers, unless they also have songwriting credits.

## 1990s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Ivor_Novello_Award_winners_and_nominees_(1990s%E2%80%932000s)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: 1990s")]

### 1990

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Ivor_Novello_Award_winners_and_nominees_(1990s%E2%80%932000s)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1990")]

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/David_Bowie_Chile.jpg/250px-David_Bowie_Chile.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:David_Bowie_Chile.jpg)

English singer-songwriter [David Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bowie "David Bowie") received the award for Outstanding Contribution to British Music.

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Patrick_Doyle%2C_Qatar_Masterclass.jpg/250px-Patrick_Doyle%2C_Qatar_Masterclass.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Patrick_Doyle,_Qatar_Masterclass.jpg)

Scottish composer [Patrick Doyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Doyle "Patrick Doyle") won Best Film Theme or Song for the song "Non Nobis, Domine" from _[Henry V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry\_V\_(1989\_film) "Henry V (1989 film)")_.

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Donna_Summer_C26796-19_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Donna_Summer_C26796-19_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Donna_Summer_C26796-19_(cropped).jpg)

[Donna Summer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donna_Summer "Donna Summer") won the award for Most Performed Work along with [Mike Stock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Stock_(musician) "Mike Stock (musician)"), [Matt Aitken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Aitken "Matt Aitken") and [Pete Waterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Waterman "Pete Waterman") for her song "[This Time I Know It's for Real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This_Time_I_Know_It's_for_Real "This Time I Know It's for Real")".

The 35th Ivor Novello Awards were presented on April 2, 1990, at the Grosvenor House, London.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Ivor_Novello_Award_winners_and_nominees_(1990s%E2%80%932000s)#cite_note-1)

English DJ [Adamski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adamski "Adamski") won Best Contemporary Song alongside [Seal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_(musician) "Seal (musician)").

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/The_Rolling_Stones_Summerfest_in_Milwaukee_-_2015.jpg/250px-The_Rolling_Stones_Summerfest_in_Milwaukee_-_2015.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Rolling_Stones_Summerfest_in_Milwaukee_-_2015.jpg)

[The Rolling Stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stones "The Rolling Stones") members [Mick Jagger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Jagger "Mick Jagger"), [Keith Richards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Richards "Keith Richards"), [Charlie Watts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Watts "Charlie Watts"), [Ronnie Wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronnie_Wood "Ronnie Wood") and [Bill Wyman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Wyman "Bill Wyman") received the award for Outstanding Contribution to British Music.

The 36th Ivor Novello Awards were presented on May 2, 1991, at the Grosvenor House, London.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Ivor_Novello_Award_winners_and_nominees_(1990s%E2%80%932000s)#cite_note-2)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The **[Ivor Novello Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards "Ivor Novello Awards")** are held annually since 1956 by the [Ivors Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ivors_Academy "The Ivors Academy"), formerly the British Academy of Songwriters, Composers and Authors, to recognize the excellence in [songwriting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songwriting "Songwriting") and [composing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_composition "Musical composition"). The following list consists of all the winners and nominees of the awards by year, the winners are listed first and in **bold** followed by the nominees if present.

The awards and nominations are received by the songwriters of the nominated work, not the performers, unless they also have songwriting credits.

## 1990s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Ivor_Novello_Award_winners_and_nominees_(1990s%E2%80%932000s)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: 1990s")]

### 1990

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Ivor_Novello_Award_winners_and_nominees_(1990s%E2%80%932000s)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1990")]

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/David_Bowie_Chile.jpg/250px-David_Bowie_Chile.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:David_Bowie_Chile.jpg)

English singer-songwriter [David Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bowie "David Bowie") received the award for Outstanding Contribution to British Music.

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Patrick_Doyle%2C_Qatar_Masterclass.jpg/250px-Patrick_Doyle%2C_Qatar_Masterclass.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Patrick_Doyle,_Qatar_Masterclass.jpg)

Scottish composer [Patrick Doyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Doyle "Patrick Doyle") won Best Film Theme or Song for the song "Non Nobis, Domine" from _[Henry V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry\_V\_(1989\_film) "Henry V (1989 film)")_.

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Donna_Summer_C26796-19_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Donna_Summer_C26796-19_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Donna_Summer_C26796-19_(cropped).jpg)

[Donna Summer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donna_Summer "Donna Summer") won the award for Most Performed Work along with [Mike Stock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Stock_(musician) "Mike Stock (musician)"), [Matt Aitken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Aitken "Matt Aitken") and [Pete Waterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Waterman "Pete Waterman") for her song "[This Time I Know It's for Real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This_Time_I_Know_It's_for_Real "This Time I Know It's for Real")".

The 35th Ivor Novello Awards were presented on April 2, 1990, at the Grosvenor House, London.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Ivor_Novello_Award_winners_and_nominees_(1990s%E2%80%932000s)#cite_note-1)

**The Ivor Novello Awards**, named after the Welsh entertainer [Ivor Novello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello "Ivor Novello"), are awards for [songwriting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songwriting "Songwriting") and [composing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_composition "Musical composition"). They have been presented annually in London by the [Ivors Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ivors_Academy "The Ivors Academy"), formerly called the [British Academy of Songwriters, Composers, and Authors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_of_Songwriters,_Composers_and_Authors "British Academy of Songwriters, Composers and Authors"), since 1956.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-about-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-BBC-2)

## Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ivor_Novello_Awards&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Awards")]

The awards are presented at two annual ceremonies known as **the Ivors**[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-3) and **the Ivors Composer Awards**.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-4)

*   **The Ivors** take place each May and, as of 2020, are sponsored by [Apple Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Music "Apple Music").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-5) They are recognised worldwide as the major platform for recognising and rewarding Britain and Ireland's songwriting and composing talents.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-BBC-2) The Ivors remain the only award ceremony in the musical calendar that is not influenced by publishers and record companies, but judged and presented by the writing community.

*   **The Ivors Composer Awards** take place each December and are sponsored by PRS for Music.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-6) They are broadcast by [BBC Radio 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_3 "BBC Radio 3").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-7)

The award itself is a solid bronze sculpture of [Euterpe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euterpe "Euterpe"), the [muse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muse "Muse") of lyric poetry.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-BBC-2) It was designed in 1955 by Hazel Underwood.

## Trivia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ivor_Novello_Awards&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Trivia")]

*   In 1964, [John Lennon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lennon "John Lennon") and [Paul McCartney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_McCartney "Paul McCartney") received four nominations for Ivors, including two nominations in the same category (as writers of both of the two songs competing for Highest British Sales of 1963), and were also given a Special Award for Outstanding Services to British Music.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-8)
*   [Lynsey de Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynsey_de_Paul "Lynsey de Paul") became the first woman to receive an Ivor Award for "[Won't Somebody Dance with Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Won't_Somebody_Dance_with_Me "Won't Somebody Dance with Me")" (The Best Ballad or Romantic Song) in 1974[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-9) and she went on to win another Ivor a year later for her TV theme song "[No Honestly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Honestly "No Honestly")".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-10)
*   In 1976, [10cc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10cc "10cc") musicians [Graham Gouldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Gouldman "Graham Gouldman") and [Eric Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Stewart "Eric Stewart") achieved three awards for writing "[I'm Not in Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'm_Not_in_Love "I'm Not in Love")" when it won them the Ivors for Most Performed British Work, for Best Pop Song, and for International Hit of the Year.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-11)
*   In 2008, [Amy Winehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amy_Winehouse "Amy Winehouse") received three nominations for Ivors, including two nominations in the same category (for Best Song Musically & Lyrically).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-13)
*   In 2010, an Ivor was awarded for the first time to a [video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game "Video game") soundtrack, the [PS3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_3 "PlayStation 3") title, _[Killzone 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killzone\_2 "Killzone 2")_, composed by [Joris de Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joris_de_Man "Joris de Man").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-14)

**The Ivor Novello Awards**, named after the Welsh entertainer [Ivor Novello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello "Ivor Novello"), are awards for [songwriting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songwriting "Songwriting") and [composing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_composition "Musical composition"). They have been presented annually in London by the [Ivors Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ivors_Academy "The Ivors Academy"), formerly called the [British Academy of Songwriters, Composers, and Authors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_of_Songwriters,_Composers_and_Authors "British Academy of Songwriters, Composers and Authors"), since 1956.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-about-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-BBC-2)

## Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ivor_Novello_Awards&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Awards")]

The awards are presented at two annual ceremonies known as **the Ivors**[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-3) and **the Ivors Composer Awards**.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-4)

*   **The Ivors** take place each May and, as of 2020, are sponsored by [Apple Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Music "Apple Music").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-5) They are recognised worldwide as the major platform for recognising and rewarding Britain and Ireland's songwriting and composing talents.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-BBC-2) The Ivors remain the only award ceremony in the musical calendar that is not influenced by publishers and record companies, but judged and presented by the writing community.

*   **The Ivors Composer Awards** take place each December and are sponsored by PRS for Music.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-6) They are broadcast by [BBC Radio 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_3 "BBC Radio 3").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-7)

The award itself is a solid bronze sculpture of [Euterpe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euterpe "Euterpe"), the [muse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muse "Muse") of lyric poetry.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-BBC-2) It was designed in 1955 by Hazel Underwood.

## Award categories

## Trivia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ivor_Novello_Awards&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Trivia")]

*   In 1964, [John Lennon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lennon "John Lennon") and [Paul McCartney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_McCartney "Paul McCartney") received four nominations for Ivors, including two nominations in the same category (as writers of both of the two songs competing for Highest British Sales of 1963), and were also given a Special Award for Outstanding Services to British Music.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-8)
*   [Lynsey de Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynsey_de_Paul "Lynsey de Paul") became the first woman to receive an Ivor Award for "[Won't Somebody Dance with Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Won't_Somebody_Dance_with_Me "Won't Somebody Dance with Me")" (The Best Ballad or Romantic Song) in 1974[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-9) and she went on to win another Ivor a year later for her TV theme song "[No Honestly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Honestly "No Honestly")".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-10)
*   In 1976, [10cc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10cc "10cc") musicians [Graham Gouldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Gouldman "Graham Gouldman") and [Eric Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Stewart "Eric Stewart") achieved three awards for writing "[I'm Not in Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'm_Not_in_Love "I'm Not in Love")" when it won them the Ivors for Most Performed British Work, for Best Pop Song, and for International Hit of the Year.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-11)
*   In 2008, [Amy Winehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amy_Winehouse "Amy Winehouse") received three nominations for Ivors, including two nominations in the same category (for Best Song Musically & Lyrically).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-13)
*   In 2010, an Ivor was awarded for the first time to a [video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game "Video game") soundtrack, the [PS3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_3 "PlayStation 3") title, _[Killzone 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killzone\_2 "Killzone 2")_, composed by [Joris de Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joris_de_Man "Joris de Man").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Novello_Awards#cite_note-14)

Musical artist

**Sir George Ivan Morrison** (born 31 August 1945) is a Northern Irish musician, singer, and songwriter whose recording career started in the 1960s. Morrison's albums have performed well in the [UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") and [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Ireland "Republic of Ireland"), with more than 40 reaching the [UK Top 40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_singles_chart "UK singles chart"), as well as internationally, including in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), and the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands").

He has scored top ten albums in the UK in four consecutive decades, following the success of 2021's _[Latest Record Project, Volume 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latest\_Record\_Project,\_Volume\_1 "Latest Record Project, Volume 1")_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-1) Eighteen of [his albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison_discography "Van Morrison discography") have reached the top 40 in the United States, twelve of them between 1997 and 2017.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-2) Since turning 70 in 2015, he has released – on average – more than an album a year. [His accolades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_awards_and_nominations_received_by_Van_Morrison "List of awards and nominations received by Van Morrison") include two [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Grammy-3) the 1994 [Brit Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brit_Award "Brit Award") for Outstanding Contribution to Music, the 2017 [Americana Music Lifetime Achievement Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americana_Music_Honors_&_Awards "Americana Music Honors & Awards") for Songwriting, and inductions into both the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") and the [Songwriters Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songwriters_Hall_of_Fame "Songwriters Hall of Fame"). In 2016 he was [knighted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight_Bachelor "Knight Bachelor") for services to the music industry and to tourism in Northern Ireland.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-5)

Morrison began performing as a teenager in the late 1950s, playing a variety of instruments including guitar, harmonica, keyboards and saxophone for various [Irish showbands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_showband "Irish showband"), covering the popular hits of that time. Known as "Van the Man" to his fans,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-6) Morrison rose to prominence in the mid-1960s as the lead singer of the [Belfast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belfast "Belfast")[R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") band [Them](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Them_(band) "Them (band)"), with whom he wrote and recorded "[Gloria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloria_(Them_song) "Gloria (Them song)")", which became a [garage band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garage_band "Garage band") staple. His solo career started under the pop-hit-oriented guidance of [Bert Berns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bert_Berns "Bert Berns") with the release of the hit single "[Brown Eyed Girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_Eyed_Girl "Brown Eyed Girl")" in 1967.

After Berns's death, [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Records "Warner Bros. Records") bought Morrison's contract and allowed him three sessions to record _[Astral Weeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astral\_Weeks "Astral Weeks")_ (1968).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-7) While initially a poor seller, the album has come to be regarded as a classic.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-8)_[Moondance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moondance "Moondance")_ (1970) established Morrison as a major artist,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-9) and he built on his reputation throughout the 1970s with a series of acclaimed albums and live performances.

Much of Morrison's music is structured around the conventions of [soul music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music") and early [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues"). An equal part of his catalogue consists of lengthy, spiritually inspired musical journeys that show the influence of Celtic tradition, jazz and [stream-of-consciousness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stream-of-consciousness "Stream-of-consciousness") narrative, of which _Astral Weeks_ is a prime example.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-VF_review-11) The two strains together are sometimes referred to as "Celtic soul",[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Astral_Weeks,_Light-12) and his music has been described as attaining "a kind of violent transcendence".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-13)

## Life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Van_Morrison&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life and career")]

### Early life and musical roots: 1945–1964

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Van_Morrison&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early life and musical roots: 1945–1964")]

George Ivan Morrison was born on 31 August 1945,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-14) at 125 [Hyndford Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyndford_Street "Hyndford Street"), [Bloomfield, Belfast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomfield,_Belfast "Bloomfield, Belfast"), Northern Ireland,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-nosurrender-15) as the only child of George Morrison, a [shipyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shipyard "Shipyard") electrician, and Violet Morrison (née Stitt), who had been a singer and [tap dancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tap_dance "Tap dance") in her youth. The previous occupant of the house was the writer [Lee Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Child "Lee Child")'s father.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Van_the_Man-16) Morrison's family were working class [Protestants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster_Protestants "Ulster Protestants") descended from the [Ulster Scots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster_Scots_people "Ulster Scots people") population that settled in Belfast.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage18-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage4-19) From 1950 to 1956, Morrison, who began to be known as "Van" during this time, attended [Elmgrove Primary School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elmgrove_Primary_School "Elmgrove Primary School").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage20-20) His father had what was at the time one of the largest record collections in Northern Ireland (acquired during his time in Detroit, Michigan, in the early 1950s)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage19-21) and the young Morrison grew up listening to artists such as [Jelly Roll Morton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jelly_Roll_Morton "Jelly Roll Morton"), [Ray Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Charles "Ray Charles"), [Lead Belly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_Belly "Lead Belly"), [Sonny Terry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Terry "Sonny Terry") and [Brownie McGhee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brownie_McGhee "Brownie McGhee") and [Solomon Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomon_Burke "Solomon Burke");[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage20-20)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage20-22) of whom he later said, "If it weren't for guys like Ray and Solomon, I wouldn't be where I am today. Those guys were the inspiration that got me going. If it wasn't for that kind of music, I couldn't do what I'm doing now."[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Renaissance_Van-23)

His father's record collection exposed him to various musical genres, such as the [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues") of [Muddy Waters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muddy_Waters "Muddy Waters"); the [gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music") of [Mahalia Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahalia_Jackson "Mahalia Jackson"); the [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") of [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"); the [folk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music") of [Woody Guthrie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woody_Guthrie "Woody Guthrie"); and [country music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") from [Hank Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hank_Williams "Hank Williams") and [Jimmie Rodgers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmie_Rodgers_(country_singer) "Jimmie Rodgers (country singer)"),[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage20-20) while the first record he ever bought was by blues musician [Sonny Terry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Terry "Sonny Terry").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Listening_Party-24) When [Lonnie Donegan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonnie_Donegan "Lonnie Donegan") had a hit with "[Rock Island Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_Island_Line_(song) "Rock Island Line (song)")", written by Huddie Ledbetter ([Lead Belly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_Belly "Lead Belly")), Morrison felt he was familiar with and able to connect with [skiffle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiffle "Skiffle") music as he had been hearing Lead Belly before that.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-CollisPage_33-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Van_Morrison_%E2%80%93_salon.com-26)

Morrison's father bought him his first acoustic guitar when he was 11, and he learned to play rudimentary [chords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_(music) "Chord (music)") from the song book _The [Carter Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter\_Family "Carter Family") Style_, edited by [Alan Lomax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Lomax "Alan Lomax").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage25-27) In 1957, at the age of twelve, Morrison formed his first band,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-28) a skiffle group, "The Sputniks", named after the satellite, [Sputnik 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_1 "Sputnik 1"), that had been launched in October of that year by the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage22-29) In 1958, the band played at some of the local cinemas, and Morrison took the lead, contributing most of the singing and arranging. Other short-lived groups followed – at 14, he formed Midnight Special, another modified skiffle band, and played at a school concert.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage25-27) Then, when he heard [Jimmy Giuffre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Giuffre "Jimmy Giuffre") playing saxophone on "The Train and The River", he talked his father into buying him a [tenor saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor_saxophone "Tenor saxophone"),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage34-30) and took saxophone and music reading lessons from jazz musician [George Cassidy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Cassidy_(jazz_musician) "George Cassidy (jazz musician)"), who Morrison saw as a "big inspiration", and they became friends, facilitated by the fact that he grew up with him living nearby, also on Hyndford Street.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage26-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-33) Now playing the saxophone, Morrison joined with various local bands, including one called Deanie Sands and the Javelins, with whom he played guitar and shared singing. The line-up of the band was lead vocalist Deanie Sands, guitarist [George Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Jones_(radio_presenter) "George Jones (radio presenter)"), and drummer and vocalist Roy Kane.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Rolling_Stone_Interview-34) Later the four main musicians of the Javelins, with the addition of Wesley Black as pianist, became known as the Monarchs.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage28-35)

Morrison attended [Orangefield Boys Secondary School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orangefield_High_School "Orangefield High School"), leaving in July 1960 with no qualifications.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-O'Hagan-36) As a member of a working-class community, he was expected to get a regular full-time job,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage28-35) so after several short apprenticeship positions, he settled into a job as a [window cleaner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Window_cleaner "Window cleaner")—later alluded to in his songs "[Cleaning Windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleaning_Windows "Cleaning Windows")" and "[Saint Dominic's Preview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Dominic's_Preview_(song) "Saint Dominic's Preview (song)")".[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-37) However, he had been developing his musical interests from an early age and continued playing with the Monarchs part-time. Young Morrison also played with the Harry Mack Showband, the Great Eight, with his older workplace friend, Geordie (G. D.) Sproule, whom he later named as one of his biggest influences.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage43-44-38)

At age 17, Morrison toured Europe for the first time with the Monarchs, now calling themselves the International Monarchs. This [Irish showband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_showband "Irish showband"),[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-39) with Morrison playing saxophone, guitar and harmonica, in addition to back-up duty on bass and drums, toured seamy clubs and US Army bases in Scotland, England and Germany, often playing five sets a night.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Rolling_Stone_Interview-34) While in Germany, the band recorded a single, "Boozoo Hully Gully"/"Twingy Baby", under the name Georgie and the Monarchs. This was Morrison's first recording, taking place in November 1963 at [Ariola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariola "Ariola") Studios in [Cologne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cologne "Cologne") with Morrison on saxophone; it made the lower reaches of the German charts.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-41)

Upon returning to Belfast in November 1963, the group disbanded,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage33-38-42) so Morrison reconnected with Geordie Sproule and played with him in the Manhattan Showband along with guitarist [Herbie Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Armstrong "Herbie Armstrong"). When Armstrong auditioned to play with Brian Rossi and the Golden Eagles, later known as [the Wheels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wheels "The Wheels"), Morrison went along and was hired as a blues singer.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-45)

### Them: 1964–1966

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Van_Morrison&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Them: 1964–1966")]

Main article: [Them (band)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Them_(band) "Them (band)")

The roots of Them, the band that first broke Morrison on the international scene, came in April 1964 when he responded to an advert for musicians to play at a new [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") club at the Maritime Hotel in College Square North– an old Belfast hostel frequented by sailors.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-47) The new club needed a band for its opening night. Morrison had left the Golden Eagles (the group with which he had been performing at the time), so he created a new band out of the Gamblers, an [East Belfast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belfast_East_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Belfast East (UK Parliament constituency)") group formed by Ronnie Millings, Billy Harrison and Alan Henderson in 1962. Morrison took the place of his friend, Bill Dunn, who left the band months earlier to become a pastor.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-The_rough_guide-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-The_Belfast_Blues-50)[Eric Wrixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Wrixon "Eric Wrixon"), still a schoolboy, was the piano player and keyboardist.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-51) Morrison played saxophone and harmonica and shared vocals with Billy Harrison. They followed Eric Wrixon's suggestion for a new name, and the Gamblers morphed into [Them](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Them_(band) "Them (band)"), their name taken from the 1954 horror movie _[Them!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Them! "Them!")_[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-52)

The band's R&B performances at the Maritime attracted attention. Them performed without a routine and Morrison [ad libbed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ad_lib "Ad lib"), creating his songs live as he performed.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage40-53) While the band did covers, they also played some of Morrison's early songs, such as "Could You Would You", which he had written in [Camden Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden_Town "Camden Town") while touring with the Manhattan Showband.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-54) The debut of Morrison's "[Gloria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloria_(Them_song) "Gloria (Them song)")" took place on stage here. Sometimes, depending on his mood, the song could last up to twenty minutes. Morrison has said, "Them lived and died on the stage at the Maritime Hotel", believing the band did not manage to capture the spontaneity and energy of their live performances on their records.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage44-55) The statement also reflected the instability of the Them line-up, with numerous members passing through the ranks after the definitive Maritime period. Morrison and Henderson remained the only constants, and a less successful version of Them soldiered on after Morrison's departure.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-56)

[Dick Rowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Rowe "Dick Rowe") of [Decca Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decca_Records "Decca Records") became aware of the band's performances and signed Them to a standard two-year contract. In that period, they released two albums and ten singles, with two more singles released after Morrison departed the band. They had three [chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_chart "Record chart") hits, "[Baby, Please Don't Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby,_Please_Don't_Go "Baby, Please Don't Go")" (1964), "[Here Comes the Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Here_Comes_the_Night_(Them_song) "Here Comes the Night (Them song)")" (1965), and "[Mystic Eyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystic_Eyes "Mystic Eyes")" (1965),[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-57) but it was the B-side of "Baby, Please Don't Go", the [garage band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garage_band "Garage band") classic "Gloria",[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage48-51-58) that went on to become a rock standard covered by [Patti Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patti_Smith "Patti Smith"), [the Doors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doors "The Doors"), [the Shadows of Knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shadows_of_Knight "The Shadows of Knight"), [Jimi Hendrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimi_Hendrix "Jimi Hendrix") and many others.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-59)

![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/60px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

[Gloria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gloria_-_Them.ogg "File:Gloria - Them.ogg")

[Audio 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/5/5a/Gloria_-_Them.ogg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=original)

Morrison's garage rock classic was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1999. As described by [Paul Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Williams_(Crawdaddy!_creator) "Paul Williams (Crawdaddy! creator)"): "Van Morrison's voice a fierce beacon in the darkness, the lighthouse at the end of the world. Resulting in one of the most perfect rock anthems known to humankind."[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-60)

* * *

_Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._

Building on the success of their singles in the United States, and riding on the back of the [British Invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Invasion "British Invasion"), Them undertook a two-month tour of America in May and June 1966 that included a residency from 30 May to 18 June at the [Whisky a Go Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whisky_a_Go_Go "Whisky a Go Go") in Los Angeles.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage65-61)[The Doors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doors "The Doors") were the supporting act on the last week,[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-62) and Morrison's influence on the Doors singer [Jim Morrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Morrison "Jim Morrison") (no relation) was noted by [John Densmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Densmore "John Densmore") in his book _Riders on the Storm_. [Brian Hinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Hinton "Brian Hinton") relates how "Jim Morrison learned quickly from his near namesake's stagecraft, his apparent recklessness, his air of subdued menace, the way he would improvise poetry to a rock beat, even his habit of crouching down by the bass drum during instrumental breaks."[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage67-63) On the final night, the two Morrisons and the two bands jammed together on "Gloria".[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-VanM-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-66)

Toward the end of the tour the band members became involved in a dispute with their manager, Decca Records' [Phil Solomon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Solomon_(music_executive) "Phil Solomon (music executive)"), over the revenues paid to them; that, coupled with the expiry of their work visas, meant the band returned from America dejected. After two more concerts in Ireland, Them split up. Morrison concentrated on writing some of the songs that would appear on _[Astral Weeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astral\_Weeks "Astral Weeks")_, while the remnants of the band reformed in 1967 and relocated to America.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage72-73-67)

### Start of solo career with Bang Records and "Brown Eyed Girl": 1967

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Van_Morrison&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Start of solo career with Bang Records and \"Brown Eyed Girl\": 1967")]

![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/60px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

[Brown Eyed Girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Van_Morrison-Brown_Eyed_Girl.ogg "File:Van Morrison-Brown Eyed Girl.ogg")

[Audio 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/c/c2/Van_Morrison-Brown_Eyed_Girl.ogg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=original)

Morrison's classic 1967 hit single which appeared on the album _Blowin' Your Mind!_. In 2007, it was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-68)

* * *

_Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._

[Bert Berns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bert_Berns "Bert Berns"), Them's producer and composer of their 1965 hit "Here Comes the Night", persuaded Morrison to return to New York to record solo for his new label, [Bang Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bang_Records "Bang Records").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPagep188-69) Morrison flew over and signed a contract he had not fully studied.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-70) During a two-day recording session at [A & R Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_&_R_Studios "A & R Studios") starting 28 March 1967, he recorded eight songs, originally intended to be used as four singles.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-71) Instead, these songs were released as the album _[Blowin' Your Mind!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blowin'\_Your\_Mind! "Blowin' Your Mind!")_ without Morrison's consultation. He said he only became aware of the album's release when a friend mentioned that he had bought a copy. Morrison was unhappy with the album and said he "had a different concept of it".[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage204-72)

"[Brown Eyed Girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_Eyed_Girl "Brown Eyed Girl")", one of the songs from _Blowin' Your Mind!_, was released as a single in mid-June 1967,[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-73) reaching number ten in the US charts. "Brown Eyed Girl" became Morrison's most-played song.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-74) The song spent a total of sixteen weeks on the chart.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-75) An evaluation in 2015 of downloads since 2004 and airplay since 2010 had "Brown Eyed Girl" as the most popular song of the entire 1960s decade.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-76) In 2000, it was listed at No.21 on the _Rolling Stone_/MTV list of 100 Greatest Pop Songs[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-77) and as No. 49 on [VH1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VH1 "VH1")'s list of the 100 Greatest Rock Songs.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-78) In 2010, "Brown Eyed Girl" was ranked No.110 on the _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ magazine list of [500 Greatest Songs of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/500_Greatest_Songs_of_All_Time "500 Greatest Songs of All Time").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RS500GRSONGS-79) In January 2007, "Brown Eyed Girl" was inducted into the [Grammy Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Hall_of_Fame "Grammy Hall of Fame").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Grammy_Hall_of_Fame-80)

Following the death of Berns in 1967, Morrison became involved in a contract dispute with Berns' widow, [Ilene Berns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilene_Berns "Ilene Berns"), that prevented him from performing on stage or recording in the New York area.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage212-215-81) The song "Big Time Operators", released in 1993, is thought to allude to his dealings with the New York [music business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_industry "Music industry") during this period.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage216-82) He moved to [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"), Massachusetts, and faced personal and financial problems; he had "slipped into a malaise" and had trouble finding concert bookings.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage217-83) He regained his professional footing through the few gigs he could find, and started recording with [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Records "Warner Bros. Records").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage170-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage176,177-85)

Warner Bros. bought out Morrison's Bang contract with a $20,000 cash transaction that took place in an abandoned warehouse on [Ninth Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninth_Avenue_(Manhattan) "Ninth Avenue (Manhattan)") in Manhattan.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-WalshPages15-19-86) A clause required Morrison to submit 36 original songs within a year to Berns' music publishing company. He recorded them in one session on an out-of-tune guitar, with lyrics about subjects including [ringworm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dermatophytosis "Dermatophytosis") and sandwiches. Ilene Berns thought the songs were "nonsense" and did not use them.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage212-222-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-88) The throwaway compositions came to be known as the "revenge" songs,[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-89) and did not see official release until the 2017 compilation _[The Authorized Bang Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Authorized\_Bang\_Collection "The Authorized Bang Collection")_.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-90)

### _Astral Weeks_: 1968

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Van_Morrison&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Astral Weeks: 1968")]

Main article: [Astral Weeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astral_Weeks "Astral Weeks")

![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/60px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

The 1968 title song featuring the opening lines of the album: "If I ventured in the slipstream between the viaducts of your dream". His early voice was described as "flinty and tender, beseeching and plaintive".[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-O'Hagan,_Sean-91)

* * *

_Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._

Morrison's first album for Warner Bros Records was _Astral Weeks_ (which he had already performed in several clubs around Boston), a mystical [song cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_cycle "Song cycle"), often considered to be his best work and one of the best albums of all time.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-AS2008-92)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-allmusicAW-93)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage223-94) Morrison has said, "When _Astral Weeks_ came out, I was starving, _literally_."[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage100-95) Released in 1968, the album originally received an indifferent response from the public, but it eventually achieved critical acclaim.

The album is described by [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic")'s William Ruhlmann as hypnotic, meditative, and as possessing a unique musical power.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-allmusicAW-93) It has been compared to French [Impressionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressionism "Impressionism") and mystical Celtic poetry.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-96)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-97)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage88,99-98) A 2004 _Rolling Stone_ magazine review begins with the words: "This is music of such enigmatic beauty that thirty-five years after its release, _Astral Weeks_ still defies easy, admiring description."[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RS19-99)[Alan Light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Light_(journalist) "Alan Light (journalist)") later described _Astral Weeks_ as "like nothing he had done previously—and really, nothing anyone had done previously. Morrison sings of lost love, death, and nostalgia for childhood in the Celtic soul that would become his signature."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Astral_Weeks,_Light-12) It has been placed on many lists of best albums of all time. In the 1995 _Mojo_ list of 100 Best Albums, it was listed as number two and was number nineteen on the _Rolling Stone_ magazine's "[500 Greatest Albums of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Albums_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time")" in 2003.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-100)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-500_Greatest_Albums-101) In December 2009, it was voted the top Irish album of all time by a poll of leading Irish musicians conducted by _[Hot Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot\_Press "Hot Press")_ magazine.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-102)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-103)

### _Moondance_ to _Into the Music_: 1970–1979

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Van_Morrison&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Moondance to Into the Music: 1970–1979")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/Van_Morrison_%281972%29.png/250px-Van_Morrison_%281972%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Van_Morrison_(1972).png)

Morrison in 1972

Morrison's third solo album, _[Moondance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moondance "Moondance")_, which was released in 1970, became his first million selling album and reached number twenty-nine on the Billboard charts.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage95-104)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage98-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-106) The style of _Moondance_ stood in contrast to that of _[Astral Weeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astral\_Weeks "Astral Weeks")_. Whereas _Astral Weeks_ had a sorrowful and vulnerable tone, _Moondance_ restored a more optimistic and cheerful message to his music,[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-YorkePage69-107) which abandoned the previous record's abstract folk compositions in favour of more formally composed songs and a lively [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") style he expanded on throughout his career.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-108)

The title track, although not released in the US as a single until 1977, received heavy play in [FM radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FM_broadcasting "FM broadcasting") formats.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage250-109) "[Into the Mystic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Into_the_Mystic "Into the Mystic")" has also gained a wide following over the years.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-allmusic_Biography:_Van_Morrison-110)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-111) "[Come Running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Come_Running "Come Running")", which reached the [American Top 40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Top_40 "American Top 40"), rescued Morrison from what seemed then as Hot 100 obscurity.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-allmusic.com-112)_Moondance_ was both well received and favourably reviewed. [Lester Bangs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Bangs "Lester Bangs") and [Greil Marcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greil_Marcus "Greil Marcus") had a combined full-page review in _Rolling Stone_, saying Morrison now had "the striking imagination of a consciousness that is visionary in the strongest sense of the word."[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Marcus,_Bangs-113) "That was the type of band I dig," Morrison said of the _Moondance_ sessions. "Two horns and a rhythm section—they're the type of bands that I like best." He produced the album himself as he felt like nobody else knew what he wanted.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage226-114)_Moondance_ was listed at number sixty-five on the _Rolling Stone_ magazine's _The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time_.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-500_Greatest_Albums-101) In March 2007, _Moondance_ was listed as number seventy-two on the [NARM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_of_Recording_Merchandisers "National Association of Recording Merchandisers")[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") list of the "Definitive 200".[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Narm-115)

Over the next few years, he released a succession of albums, starting with a second one in 1970. _[His Band and the Street Choir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/His\_Band\_and\_the\_Street\_Choir "His Band and the Street Choir")_ had a freer, more relaxed sound than _Moondance_, but not the _perfection_, in the opinion of critic [Jon Landau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Landau "Jon Landau"), who felt like "a few more numbers with a gravity of 'Street Choir' would have made this album as perfect as anyone could have stood."[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HBATSC-116) It contained the hit single "[Domino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domino_(Van_Morrison_song) "Domino (Van Morrison song)")", which charted at number nine in the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100").[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-CollisPage122-117)

In 1971, he released another well-received album, _[Tupelo Honey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tupelo\_Honey "Tupelo Honey")_.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage259-118) This album produced the hit single "[Wild Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_Night "Wild Night")" that was later covered by [John Mellencamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mellencamp "John Mellencamp") and [Meshell Ndegeocello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meshell_Ndegeocello "Meshell Ndegeocello"). The title song has a notably country-soul feel about it[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-119) and the album ended with another country tune, "[Moonshine Whiskey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonshine_Whiskey "Moonshine Whiskey")". Morrison said he originally intended to make an all-country album.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage267-268-120) The recordings were as live as possible—after rehearsing the songs the musicians would enter the studio and play a whole set in one take.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-121) His co-producer, [Ted Templeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Templeman "Ted Templeman"), described this recording process as the "scariest thing I've ever seen. When he's got something together, he wants to put it down right away with no overdubbing."[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage137-122)

Released in 1972, _[Saint Dominic's Preview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint\_Dominic's\_Preview "Saint Dominic's Preview")_ revealed Morrison's break from the more accessible style of his previous three albums and moving back towards the more daring, adventurous, and meditative aspects of _Astral Weeks_. The combination of two styles of music demonstrated a versatility not previously found in his earlier albums.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Saint_Dominic's_Preview_Music_Review-123) Two songs, "[Jackie Wilson Said (I'm in Heaven When You Smile)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Wilson_Said_(I'm_in_Heaven_When_You_Smile) "Jackie Wilson Said (I'm in Heaven When You Smile)")" and "[Redwood Tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redwood_Tree_(song) "Redwood Tree (song)")", reached the Hot 100 singles chart.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-allmusic.com-112) The songs "[Listen to the Lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listen_to_the_Lion "Listen to the Lion")" and "[Almost Independence Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_Independence_Day "Almost Independence Day")" are each over ten minutes long and employ the type of poetic imagery not heard since _Astral Weeks_.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Saint_Dominic's_Preview_Music_Review-123)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage255-256-124) It was his highest-charting album in the US until his Top Ten debut on [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") in 2008.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Charts_&_Awards-125)

He released his next album, _[Hard Nose the Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard\_Nose\_the\_Highway "Hard Nose the Highway")_, in 1973, receiving mixed, but mostly negative, reviews. The album contained the popular song "[Warm Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warm_Love "Warm Love")" but otherwise has been largely dismissed critically.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage265-267-126) In a 1973 _Rolling Stone_ review, it was described as: "psychologically complex, musically somewhat uneven and lyrically excellent."[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HNTH-127)

During a three-week vacation visit to Ireland in October 1973, Morrison wrote seven of the songs that made up his next album, _[Veedon Fleece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veedon\_Fleece "Veedon Fleece")_.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage122-128) Though it attracted scant initial attention, its critical stature grew markedly over the years—with _Veedon Fleece_ now often considered to be one of Morrison's most impressive and poetic works.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage301-129)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-130) In a 2008 _Rolling Stone_ review, Andy Greene writes that when released in late 1974: "it was greeted by a collective shrug by the rock critical establishment" and concludes: "He's released many wonderful albums since, but he's never again hit the majestic heights of this one."[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Veedon_Fleece-131) "[You Don't Pull No Punches, but You Don't Push the River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Don't_Pull_No_Punches,_but_You_Don't_Push_the_River "You Don't Pull No Punches, but You Don't Push the River")", one of the album's side closers, exemplifies the long, hypnotic, cryptic Morrison with its references to visionary poet [William Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake") and to the seemingly [Grail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Grail "Holy Grail")-like Veedon Fleece object.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage300-132)

Morrison took three years to release a follow-up album. After a decade without taking time off, he said in an interview, he needed to get away from music completely and ceased listening to it for several months.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage306-133) Also suffering from [writer's block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writer's_block "Writer's block"), he seriously considered leaving the music business for good.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage305-134) Speculation that an extended [jam session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jam_session "Jam session") would be released either under the title _Mechanical Bliss_, or _Naked in the Jungle_, or _Stiff Upper Lip_, came to nothing,[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPages304-306-135) and Morrison's next album was _[A Period of Transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Period\_of\_Transition "A Period of Transition")_ in 1977, a collaboration with [Dr. John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._John "Dr. John"), who had appeared at _[The Last Waltz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Last\_Waltz "The Last Waltz")_ concert with Morrison in 1976. The album received a mild critical reception and marked the beginning of a very prolific period of song-making.

> _[Into the Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Into\_the\_Music "Into the Music")_: The album's last four songs, "Angelou", "And the Healing Has Begun", and "It's All in the Game/You Know What They're Writing About" are a veritable tour-de-force with Morrison summoning every vocal trick at his disposal from Angelou's climactic shouts to the sexually-charged, half-mumbled monologue in "And the Healing Has Begun" to the barely audible whisper that is the album's final sound.
